kernelIdea: ℂ = {a + bi | a,b ∈ ℝ} with i² = −1. Re(z) = a and Im(z) = b are both real. ℝ ⊆ ℂ via a = a + 0i, completing the tower ℕ ⊆ ℤ ⊆ ℚ ⊆ ℝ ⊆ ℂ.

kernels.l1: A complex number is two instructions: go across, then turn.
kernels.l2: A complex number is a pair of instructions — how far across, and how far up. Every ordinary number is one of these with no up at all.
kernels.l3: A complex number is written a + bi, where a and b are ordinary numbers and i is the new number with i × i = −1. Every ordinary number is a complex number with b = 0.
kernels.l4: ℂ = {a + bi | a, b ∈ ℝ}, where i² = −1. Re(z) = a and Im(z) = b are both real numbers. ℝ ⊆ ℂ via a = a + 0i, completing ℕ ⊆ ℤ ⊆ ℚ ⊆ ℝ ⊆ ℂ.
kernels.l5: A complex number is determined by its real and imaginary parts, both of which are real; ℂ contains ℝ as the numbers with zero imaginary part.
kernels.l6: ℂ is ℝ² with a multiplication; Re and Im are real-valued functions on ℂ, and ℂ carries no order compatible with its arithmetic.
kernels.l7: ℂ = {a + bi : a,b ∈ ℝ} with i² = −1; Re(z) and Im(z) are real numbers, ℝ embeds as the numbers with Im = 0, and ℂ admits no compatible order.
kernels.l8: ℂ is ℝ[x]/(x² + 1), a two-dimensional real algebra; the tower ℕ ⊆ ℤ ⊆ ℚ ⊆ ℝ ⊆ ℂ is a chain of canonical embeddings, each fixing a defect of the previous system.

kernel: ℂ = {a + bi | a,b ∈ ℝ} with i² = −1. Re(z) = a, Im(z) = b, and both are real. ℝ ⊆ ℂ via a = a + 0i, giving ℕ ⊆ ℤ ⊆ ℚ ⊆ ℝ ⊆ ℂ.
